questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: A map has a scale of 1:25,000. What actual ground distance, in kilometres, does a distance of 8 cm on the map represent?
questions.explanation: Ground distance = 8 cm x 25,000 = 200,000 cm = 2,000 m = 2 km.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: Two towns are 12 km apart on the ground. On a map of scale 1:60,000, what distance, in centimetres, should separate them?

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: A rectangular farm measures 6 cm by 4 cm on a map drawn to a scale of 1:10,000. What is the actual area of the farm in square kilometres?
questions.explanation: Actual length = 6cm x 10,000 = 60,000cm = 0.6km; width = 4cm x 10,000 = 40,000cm = 0.4km; area = 0.6 x 0.4 = 0.24 km^2.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: A map is enlarged from a scale of 1:100,000 to a scale of 1:25,000. By what factor has the linear scale of the map increased?
questions.explanation: The linear enlargement factor = old denominator / new denominator = 100,000 / 25,000 = 4.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: A map originally at a scale of 1:20,000 is reduced so that its new scale becomes 1:80,000. By what factor has the map's linear scale been reduced?
questions.explanation: Reduction factor = new denominator / old denominator = 80,000 / 20,000 = 4.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: The bearing of a village Q from a village P is 128 degrees. What is the bearing of P from Q?
questions.explanation: Since the given bearing (128 degrees) is less than 180 degrees, the back bearing is found by adding 180 degrees: 128 + 180 = 308 degrees.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: The bearing of a hilltop R from a camp S is 205 degrees. What is the back bearing of S from R?
questions.explanation: Since the given bearing (205 degrees) exceeds 180 degrees, the back bearing is found by subtracting 180 degrees: 205 - 180 = 25 degrees.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: A surveyor stands at point A and observes point B on a bearing of N40E. Expressed in three-figure bearing notation, this is
questions.explanation: N40E means 40 degrees measured clockwise from North toward East, which converts directly to a three-figure bearing of 040 degrees.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: A hiker walks on a bearing of S30W from a starting point. Expressed in three-figure bearing notation, this direction is
questions.explanation: South is 180 degrees; turning 30 degrees toward West (i.e., toward 270) gives 180 + 30 = 210 degrees.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: On a topographical map, contour lines that form concentric closed loops with values increasing inward most likely represent a
questions.explanation: Concentric closed contours with height values increasing toward the centre indicate rising ground, characteristic of a hill or summit.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: On a topographical map, V-shaped contour lines that point toward higher ground, with the V's apex indicating the upstream direction, most likely represent a
questions.explanation: V-shaped contours pointing upstream (toward higher ground) are the classic signature of a river valley cut into the landscape.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: Two points on a map have a height difference of 60 m and are 3 km apart horizontally. What is the gradient between them, expressed as a ratio?
questions.explanation: Convert 3 km to 3,000 m; gradient = height difference / horizontal distance = 60/3,000 = 1/50, i.e. 1:50.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: The gradient between two points is given as 1:40, and the horizontal distance between them is 2 km. What is the difference in height between the points?
questions.explanation: Horizontal distance = 2,000 m; height difference = horizontal distance / gradient denominator = 2,000/40 = 50 m.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: A vertical interval (contour interval) on a map is 20 m, and there are 5 contour lines between two points on a uniform slope. What is the total difference in height between the two points?
questions.explanation: Total height difference = number of contour intervals crossed x vertical interval = 5 x 20 = 100 m.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: Which method of estimating irregular area on a map involves overlaying a grid of known unit squares and counting full and partial squares covered by the feature?
questions.explanation: The grid square method superimposes a grid of known unit area over the feature and estimates total area from the number of squares (full and part) it covers.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: A cross-section drawn between two points on a topographical map is primarily used to show the
options: profile (shape) of the relief along a given line
compass bearing between the two points
questions.explanation: A cross-section transfers height values from contour lines along a chosen line to produce a side-on profile showing how the relief rises and falls.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: In practical surveying, the instrument traditionally used to measure horizontal and vertical angles precisely is the
questions.explanation: A theodolite is a precision optical instrument used in land surveying to measure horizontal and vertical angles accurately.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: A Global Positioning System (GPS) receiver is primarily used in fieldwork to determine a
options: location's precise coordinates (latitude, longitude and elevation)
questions.explanation: GPS receivers use signals from orbiting satellites to calculate a precise position on the Earth's surface, given as latitude, longitude, and often elevation.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: In a Geographic Information System (GIS), different types of spatial data (such as roads, rivers and settlements) stored separately but able to be viewed together are referred to as
questions.explanation: GIS organises spatial data into separate thematic layers (e.g., roads, hydrology, land use) that can be overlaid and analysed together.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: Remote sensing, as used in modern geographic data collection, refers to the
options: physical measurement of land using a chain and compass on the ground
calculation of gradient using contour lines
gathering of information about the Earth's surface from a distance, typically via satellites or aircraft
collection of population data through household surveys
questions.explanation: Remote sensing involves collecting data about the Earth's surface without direct physical contact, most commonly using sensors mounted on satellites or aircraft.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: On a topographical map, a triangulation station (trig point) is significant because it
options: provides a fixed, precisely surveyed reference point of known height and location
marks the exact centre of a town's market
indicates the location of a river confluence only
shows the boundary of a forest reserve only
questions.explanation: Triangulation stations are precisely surveyed points of known coordinates and elevation that serve as fixed reference points for accurate map-making.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: If the distance between two settlements measured on a map is 3.5 cm, and the map scale is 1:200,000, what is the actual ground distance in kilometres?
questions.explanation: Ground distance = 3.5 cm x 200,000 = 700,000 cm = 7,000 m = 7 km.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: A place X is located at longitude 75 degrees East. If it is 6:00 am GMT at Greenwich, what is the local time at X?
questions.explanation: Time difference = 75/15 = 5 hours ahead of GMT (east of Greenwich); 6:00 am + 5 hours = 11:00 am.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: A town Y is located at longitude 105 degrees West. If it is 2:00 pm GMT at Greenwich, what is the local time at Y?
questions.explanation: Time difference = 105/15 = 7 hours behind GMT (west of Greenwich); 2:00 pm - 7 hours = 7:00 am.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: Two towns, P and Q, are on the same latitude. Town P is at longitude 20 degrees East and town Q is at longitude 50 degrees West. What is the local time difference between them?
questions.explanation: Total longitude difference = 20 + 50 = 70 degrees; time difference = 70 x 4 minutes = 280 minutes = 4 hours 40 minutes.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: A ship's captain notes that the local time at his position is 3:00 pm while the GMT (0 degrees longitude) time is 9:00 am on the same day. Assuming the ship is east of Greenwich, at what longitude is the ship located?
questions.explanation: Time ahead of GMT = 3:00 pm - 9:00 am = 6 hours; longitude = 6 x 15 = 90 degrees East.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: A city is 8 hours behind GMT. What is its approximate longitude, and in which direction from Greenwich?
questions.explanation: Longitude = time difference x 15 = 8 x 15 = 120 degrees; being behind GMT places it west of Greenwich.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: If it is 4:00 pm on Monday at longitude 0 degrees (GMT), what day and time is it at a location on longitude 165 degrees East?
questions.explanation: Time difference = 165/15 = 11 hours ahead; 4:00 pm (16:00) Monday + 11 hours = 27:00, which is 03:00 the next day, i.e. Tuesday 3:00 am.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: Every 1 degree of longitude corresponds to a time difference of approximately
questions.explanation: Since 15 degrees of longitude equals 1 hour (60 minutes), 1 degree of longitude equals 60/15 = 4 minutes.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: The International Date Line is located approximately along the
options: 180 degree meridian in the Pacific Ocean
questions.explanation: The International Date Line broadly follows the 180 degree meridian, running through the Pacific Ocean, with deviations to avoid splitting some land areas and island groups.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: Crossing the International Date Line while travelling from east to west (e.g., from the USA toward Asia) requires a traveller to
options: set the calendar back by one day
adjust the clock by exactly 12 hours only, with no date change
advance the calendar by one day
questions.explanation: Travelling westward across the International Date Line moves a traveller into a new calendar day, so the date is advanced by one day.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: The Earth completes one full rotation on its axis, relative to the sun, in approximately
questions.explanation: The Earth's rotation on its axis, producing the day-night cycle, takes approximately 24 hours (one solar day).

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: The Earth's revolution around the sun takes approximately how long to complete one full orbit?
questions.explanation: One complete orbit of the Earth around the sun (one year) takes approximately 365.25 days, which is why an extra day is added every four years (leap year).

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: The tilt of the Earth's axis, at approximately 23.5 degrees to the vertical of its orbital plane, is primarily responsible for
options: the daily occurrence of day and night
the changing seasons experienced at different times of the year
questions.explanation: Because the Earth's axis is tilted, different hemispheres receive more or less direct sunlight at different points in the orbit, producing the cycle of seasons.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: During the June solstice, the sun's overhead (vertical) rays are directly above which line of latitude?
options: The Tropic of Capricorn (23.5 degrees South)
The Tropic of Cancer (23.5 degrees North)
questions.explanation: At the June solstice, the Northern Hemisphere is tilted most directly toward the sun, placing the sun's overhead rays on the Tropic of Cancer.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: During the December solstice, the sun's overhead (vertical) rays are directly above which line of latitude?
options: The Tropic of Cancer (23.5 degrees North)
The Tropic of Capricorn (23.5 degrees South)
questions.explanation: At the December solstice, the Southern Hemisphere is tilted most directly toward the sun, placing the sun's overhead rays on the Tropic of Capricorn.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: At the equinoxes (around 21 March and 23 September), the sun's overhead rays fall directly on the
questions.explanation: At the equinoxes, the Earth's axis is not tilted toward or away from the sun relative to its orbit, so the overhead rays fall directly on the Equator, giving roughly equal day and night length globally.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: Latitude is measured as an angular distance north or south of the
questions.explanation: Latitude measures angular distance north or south of the Equator (0 degrees), ranging from 0 degrees at the Equator to 90 degrees at the poles.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: Longitude is measured as an angular distance east or west of the
questions.explanation: Longitude measures angular distance east or west of the Prime Meridian (0 degrees), which passes through Greenwich, England.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: The layer of the Earth's internal structure that is liquid and generates the Earth's magnetic field is the
questions.explanation: The outer core consists of molten liquid iron and nickel; its convective motion, combined with Earth's rotation, generates the planet's magnetic field.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: Which layer of the Earth lies directly beneath the crust and makes up the largest proportion of the Earth's total volume?
questions.explanation: The mantle, lying beneath the crust and above the outer core, is by far the thickest layer, making up the largest share of the Earth's total volume.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: If two towns lie on the same meridian of longitude but different latitudes, and are 555 km apart along the meridian (1 degree of latitude approx. 111 km), what is the difference in latitude between them?
questions.explanation: Difference in latitude = distance / 111 km = 555/111 = 5 degrees.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: Rocks formed from the solidification of magma while still beneath the Earth's surface (rather than at the surface) are classified as
questions.explanation: Intrusive (plutonic) igneous rocks, such as granite, cool slowly beneath the surface, allowing large crystals to form, unlike extrusive rocks that cool rapidly at the surface.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: Rocks formed from lava that cools and solidifies rapidly on the Earth's surface are classified as
questions.explanation: Extrusive (volcanic) igneous rocks, such as basalt, form when lava cools quickly at or near the Earth's surface, typically producing fine-grained crystals.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: Which of the following processes is NOT directly involved in the formation of sedimentary rocks?
options: Compaction and cementation of sediment layers
questions.explanation: Crystallisation from molten magma is the process that forms igneous rocks, not sedimentary rocks, which form through weathering, transport, deposition, compaction and cementation.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: The process by which rocks are broken down in situ (in their original place) by physical, chemical, or biological agents, without significant movement of the resulting fragments, is called
questions.explanation: Weathering is the in-situ breakdown of rocks at or near the Earth's surface, distinct from erosion, which involves the removal and transport of the resulting material.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: The process by which weathered material is removed from its original location and carried elsewhere by agents such as water, wind, or ice is called
questions.explanation: Erosion involves the wearing away and removal of surface material by natural agents like rivers, wind, waves, or glaciers, and its transport elsewhere.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: Frost shattering (freeze-thaw weathering) occurs mainly through the
options: growth of plant roots within rock crevices
repeated freezing and expansion of water within rock cracks, gradually widening and breaking them apart
chemical dissolution of rock by acidic rainwater
abrasive action of windblown sand particles
questions.explanation: Frost shattering occurs when water seeps into rock cracks, freezes and expands by about 9%, exerting pressure that gradually widens the cracks until fragments break off.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: Which of the following is an example of chemical weathering?
options: Frost shattering caused by repeated freeze-thaw cycles
Carbonation, where slightly acidic rainwater dissolves calcium carbonate in limestone
Exfoliation caused by daily temperature changes
questions.explanation: Carbonation is a chemical weathering process in which carbonic acid (formed from rainwater and atmospheric CO2) reacts with and dissolves minerals such as calcium carbonate in limestone.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: A fold in rock strata where the layers are arched upward, with the oldest rocks at the centre, is called an
questions.explanation: An anticline is an upward (convex) fold in layered rock, with the oldest rock layers exposed at its centre or core.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: A fold in rock strata where the layers are bent downward into a trough shape, with the youngest rocks at the centre, is called a
questions.explanation: A syncline is a downward (concave) fold in layered rock, with the youngest rock layers found at its centre.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: A block of the Earth's crust that has been uplifted relative to the surrounding land along fault lines, forming a plateau-like landform, is known as a
questions.explanation: A horst is an elevated block of crust bounded by parallel faults, uplifted relative to the surrounding land, often forming plateaus or block mountains.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: A depressed block of the Earth's crust that has subsided relative to the surrounding land along parallel faults, often forming a rift valley, is known as a
questions.explanation: A graben is a block of crust that has dropped down relative to the surrounding land between parallel faults, commonly forming rift valleys such as the East African Rift.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: The upper course of a river is generally characterised by
options: a gentle gradient with extensive meandering and floodplain deposition
a wide estuary with tidal influence
steep gradient, strong vertical (downward) erosion, and a narrow V-shaped valley
the formation of a delta at the river mouth
questions.explanation: In its upper course, a river typically flows down a steep gradient, with erosion dominated by vertical downcutting, producing a narrow, steep-sided V-shaped valley.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: The lower course of a river, close to its mouth, is generally characterised by
options: predominantly vertical erosion cutting a deep gorge
a gentle gradient, dominant lateral erosion and deposition, and a broad floodplain
a steep gradient with waterfalls and rapids
questions.explanation: In its lower course, a river flows over a gentle gradient with reduced energy, favouring lateral erosion, meandering, and deposition across a broad floodplain.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: An oxbow lake is formed when
options: a glacier melts and leaves behind a depression
a river's mouth is blocked by a sandbar
a meander loop is cut off from the main river channel, typically by erosion narrowing its neck
a waterfall retreats upstream over time
questions.explanation: An oxbow lake forms when continued erosion narrows the neck of a meander loop until the river cuts through it directly, isolating the loop as a crescent-shaped lake.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: A river's floodplain is best described as the
options: narrow channel cut directly into solid bedrock
point where a river meets the sea
steep-sided valley found only in a river's upper course
flat land bordering a river that is periodically covered by floodwater and receives deposited sediment
questions.explanation: A floodplain is the relatively flat area of land adjacent to a river's lower and middle course, periodically inundated during floods and built up by deposited alluvium.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: Glacial erosion in mountainous areas commonly produces a bowl-shaped hollow at the head of a valley, known as a
questions.explanation: A cirque, or corrie, is a bowl-shaped depression carved by glacial erosion at the head of a glaciated valley, often containing a small lake after the ice retreats.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: A spit, a coastal depositional landform, typically forms where
options: waves erode a headland into a narrow arch
longshore drift deposits sand or shingle in a narrow ridge extending from the coast, often at a bend or river mouth
a river deposits sediment at its mouth into a lake
glacial ice erodes a U-shaped valley
questions.explanation: A spit forms when longshore drift transports and deposits sand or shingle along the coast, building a narrow finger of land that projects out from the shoreline, often across a bay or river mouth.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: A stack, a coastal erosional landform, is best described as
options: a flat platform of rock exposed at low tide
a ridge of sand deposited parallel to the coast
a narrow inlet formed by river erosion
an isolated pillar of rock left standing offshore after the collapse of an arch
questions.explanation: A stack is formed when continued wave erosion causes a coastal arch to collapse, leaving an isolated pillar of resistant rock standing separately from the cliff.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: Which sequence correctly represents the typical stages of coastal erosion leading to the formation of a stack?
options: Headland to cave to arch to stack
Stack to arch to cave to headland
Cave to headland to stack to arch
Arch to headland to cave to stack
questions.explanation: Wave erosion progressively enlarges cracks in a headland into caves, which may erode through to form an arch; continued erosion collapses the arch's roof, leaving an isolated stack.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: Volcanic activity that occurs where two tectonic plates move apart from one another (a divergent boundary) is best exemplified by
options: the East African Rift Valley escarpments alone
questions.explanation: The Mid-Atlantic Ridge is a divergent plate boundary where the Eurasian/African and American plates move apart, allowing magma to rise and form new oceanic crust and associated volcanic activity.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: Fold mountains, such as the Himalayas, are typically formed as a result of
options: the collision of two tectonic plates, compressing and folding sedimentary rock layers upward
wind erosion of a plateau over a long period
volcanic eruptions building up layers of ash and lava alone
the gradual deposition of river sediment over millions of years
questions.explanation: Fold mountains form where converging tectonic plates collide, compressing and buckling accumulated sedimentary rock layers upward into extensive mountain ranges.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: Which weather instrument is specifically used to measure the duration of bright sunshine received at a location?
questions.explanation: A sunshine recorder, such as the Campbell-Stokes recorder, uses a glass sphere to focus sunlight and burn a trace on a card, recording the duration of bright sunshine.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: A wind vane is a weather instrument used specifically to indicate the
options: direction from which the wind is blowing
questions.explanation: A wind vane rotates freely and aligns with the wind, pointing to indicate the direction from which the wind is blowing.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: The Koppen climate classification uses the letter code 'A' to represent which broad climate group?
questions.explanation: In the Koppen system, the letter 'A' designates tropical climates, generally characterised by high temperatures throughout the year.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: The Koppen climate classification uses the letter code 'B' to represent which broad climate group?
questions.explanation: In the Koppen system, the letter 'B' designates arid (dry) climates, characterised by potential evaporation exceeding precipitation.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: A tropical monsoon climate (classified as Am under Koppen's system) is generally characterised by
options: an extended, pronounced dry season lasting most of the year
high temperatures with a short dry season but very heavy total annual rainfall
cold winters and mild, wet summers
consistently low temperatures with minimal precipitation
questions.explanation: The tropical monsoon climate features high year-round temperatures and a brief drier period, but still receives very heavy total annual rainfall, often driven by seasonal monsoon winds.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: The tropical savanna climate (classified as Aw under Koppen's system) is generally characterised by
options: no seasonal variation in rainfall whatsoever
a distinct wet and dry season, with lower total rainfall than the tropical rainforest climate
questions.explanation: The tropical savanna (Aw) climate has a pronounced wet and dry season, with total annual rainfall generally lower than that of the more consistently wet tropical rainforest (Af) climate.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: Trade winds are a persistent global wind system that generally blow from the
options: subtropical high-pressure belts toward the equatorial low-pressure belt
polar regions directly toward the equator without deflection
west toward the east at all latitudes
questions.explanation: Trade winds blow from the subtropical high-pressure belts (around 30 degrees N/S) toward the low-pressure zone near the Equator, deflected by the Coriolis effect.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: The Inter-Tropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ) is best described as the
options: zone of permanent high pressure over the poles
line marking the boundary between day and night
boundary between temperate and polar climate zones
zone near the Equator where the northeast and southeast trade winds converge, associated with rising air and heavy rainfall
questions.explanation: The ITCZ is a low-pressure belt near the Equator where trade winds from both hemispheres converge, causing air to rise, cool, and condense, producing frequent heavy rainfall.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: The general movement of the Inter-Tropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ) with the seasons is best described as
options: remaining permanently fixed exactly at the Equator throughout the year
moving only in the Southern Hemisphere year-round
shifting north and south of the Equator following the sun's apparent overhead position through the year
moving only westward across the globe over the year
questions.explanation: The ITCZ migrates seasonally, tracking the sun's apparent overhead position, moving further north in the northern summer and further south in the southern summer.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: The Gulf Stream, a well-known warm ocean current, most directly influences the climate of which region?
questions.explanation: The Gulf Stream carries warm water from the Gulf of Mexico across the Atlantic, moderating the climate of north-western Europe and keeping winters milder than the latitude would otherwise suggest.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: The cold Canary Current, flowing along the north-western coast of Africa, tends to have which effect on the adjacent coastal climate?
options: It lowers coastal temperatures and reduces rainfall, contributing to arid conditions
It has no measurable influence on the coastal climate
It causes exceptionally heavy tropical rainfall along the coast
questions.explanation: Like other cold currents, the Canary Current cools coastal air and suppresses convection, contributing to the arid conditions found along parts of the adjacent north-west African coast.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: Ocean salinity refers to the
options: temperature of ocean water at a given depth
depth of the ocean floor at a given point
speed at which ocean currents flow
concentration of dissolved salts present in seawater
questions.explanation: Salinity measures the total concentration of dissolved salts (mainly sodium chloride) in seawater, usually expressed in parts per thousand.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: An ecosystem is best defined as a
options: single species of plant or animal found in a given area
region defined purely by its political boundaries
community of living organisms interacting with each other and with their non-living physical environment
collection of rock types found in a particular area
questions.explanation: An ecosystem comprises all the living organisms (biotic factors) in an area, together with the non-living physical environment (abiotic factors), and the interactions between them.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: In an ecosystem's food chain, organisms that produce their own food through photosynthesis, forming the base of the chain, are known as
questions.explanation: Producers, mainly green plants and algae, use photosynthesis to convert sunlight into chemical energy, forming the foundation of virtually all food chains.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: Organisms that break down dead organic matter, returning nutrients to the ecosystem, are known as
questions.explanation: Decomposers, such as bacteria and fungi, break down dead plant and animal matter, releasing nutrients back into the soil and completing the nutrient cycle.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: Biodiversity refers to the
options: number of rock types present in a region
total population of a single dominant species
total mass of vegetation found in a rainforest alone
variety of living species and ecosystems found within a given area
questions.explanation: Biodiversity describes the full range of variety among living organisms, including species diversity, genetic diversity, and ecosystem diversity, within a given area.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: Laterite soils, common in many tropical regions including much of Nigeria, are formed primarily through the process of
options: the freezing and thawing of soil in polar regions
intense leaching of soluble minerals under high rainfall and temperature, leaving behind iron and aluminium oxides
the accumulation of windblown sand in arid regions
questions.explanation: Laterite soils form under intense tropical weathering and leaching, which removes soluble minerals like silica, leaving behind insoluble iron and aluminium oxides that give the soil its characteristic reddish colour.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: Soil erosion is best described as the
options: compaction of soil particles by heavy machinery alone
removal of the topsoil layer by agents such as water and wind, often accelerated by human activity
chemical enrichment of soil through fertiliser application
natural formation of new topsoil through weathering
questions.explanation: Soil erosion involves the detachment and removal of topsoil by natural agents like water and wind, a process significantly accelerated by human activities such as deforestation and poor farming practices.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: Which farming practice is commonly recommended to reduce soil erosion on sloped agricultural land?
options: Ploughing directly up and down the slope
Complete removal of all vegetation cover
questions.explanation: Terracing and contour ploughing follow the natural contours of sloped land, slowing water runoff and significantly reducing the rate of soil erosion compared to ploughing straight up and down a slope.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: Overgrazing, a significant driver of land degradation in many semi-arid regions, refers to
options: the rotation of crops to preserve soil fertility
the planting of too many trees in a small area
the fencing off of land to prevent any livestock access
excessive grazing by livestock beyond the land's capacity to regenerate vegetation
questions.explanation: Overgrazing occurs when livestock numbers exceed what the land's vegetation can sustainably support, preventing plants from regenerating and leading to soil exposure and degradation.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: Which of the following is a commonly recommended strategy for combating desertification in semi-arid regions?
options: Complete removal of windbreaks and shelterbelts
Afforestation (tree planting) and controlled grazing management
Increasing the intensity of livestock grazing
questions.explanation: Afforestation helps stabilise soil and reduce wind erosion, while controlled grazing management prevents overgrazing, both of which are key strategies for combating and reversing desertification.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: The crude birth rate of a population is defined as the
options: number of live births per 1,000 people in a population in a given year
number of deaths per 1,000 people in a population in a given year
difference between births and deaths in a population
total number of births recorded over a person's lifetime
questions.explanation: Crude birth rate is a standard demographic measure expressing the number of live births occurring per 1,000 people in a population during a specified year.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: The crude death rate of a population is defined as the
options: number of deaths per 1,000 people in a population in a given year
number of births per 1,000 people in a population in a given year
percentage of elderly people within a total population
total number of deaths recorded since a country's founding
questions.explanation: Crude death rate is a standard demographic measure expressing the number of deaths occurring per 1,000 people in a population during a specified year.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: The natural increase of a population is calculated as the
options: difference between the birth rate and the death rate
difference between urban and rural population totals
sum of the birth rate and the death rate
total number of immigrants entering a country
questions.explanation: Natural increase (or decrease) is calculated by subtracting the death rate from the birth rate, indicating how much a population is growing (or shrinking) due to births and deaths alone, excluding migration.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: A population pyramid with a narrow base and a broad, roughly even distribution through most age groups typically indicates a population with
options: very high birth rates and a large young population
a population entirely made up of young children
low birth rates and a more balanced, ageing population structure
a rapidly growing population with high fertility
questions.explanation: A narrow-based population pyramid with a more even spread across older age groups reflects low birth rates and a more mature, slower-growing (or ageing) population, typical of many developed countries.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: Population density is calculated as the
options: total birth rate minus the total death rate
number of cities within a country
total land area of a country divided by its population
total population of an area divided by its total land area
questions.explanation: Population density is expressed as the number of people per unit of land area (e.g., persons per square kilometre), calculated by dividing total population by total land area.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: Which of the following physical factors would most likely encourage a HIGH population density in a given region?
options: Permanently frozen ground unsuitable for farming
Extremely mountainous terrain with thin, infertile soil
Fertile soil, adequate rainfall, and gentle relief
A hot desert climate with minimal rainfall
questions.explanation: Fertile soils, reliable rainfall, and gentle relief generally support productive agriculture and easier settlement, encouraging denser human population concentrations.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: Internal migration, unlike international migration, refers to the movement of people
options: only for the purposes of international tourism
only from one continent to another
within the boundaries of a single country
questions.explanation: Internal migration involves the movement of people from one location to another within the same country's borders, distinct from international migration, which crosses national boundaries.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: Which of the following is most likely to act as a 'pull factor' attracting migrants to a large city?
options: A complete lack of infrastructure in the destination area
Severe drought and famine conditions in the destination area
The availability of employment opportunities and better social amenities
Ongoing armed conflict in the destination area
questions.explanation: Pull factors are attractive conditions at the destination, such as better job prospects, higher wages, and improved access to services, that draw migrants toward a location.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: Which of the following is most likely to act as a 'push factor' driving migrants away from a rural area?
options: Excellent healthcare and educational facilities locally
Limited employment opportunities and poor access to social services
A stable and prosperous local economy
questions.explanation: Push factors are unfavourable conditions at the place of origin, such as limited jobs, poverty, or poor services, that encourage people to leave in search of better conditions elsewhere.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: Nigeria's total land boundary is shared with which combination of neighbouring countries?
questions.explanation: Nigeria shares international land borders with the Republic of Benin to the west, Niger to the north, Chad to the north-east, and Cameroon to the east.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: The vegetation belt found immediately along Nigeria's coastline, characterised by salt-tolerant trees adapted to tidal, brackish water, is the
questions.explanation: Mangrove swamp forest, with its characteristic salt-tolerant trees, occupies the low-lying, tidal coastal fringe of southern Nigeria.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: Moving northward from Nigeria's coast toward the far north, the general sequence of natural vegetation belts is
options: sahel savanna, sudan savanna, guinea savanna, tropical rainforest, mangrove swamp
tropical rainforest, sahel savanna, mangrove swamp, guinea savanna
mangrove swamp, tropical rainforest, guinea savanna, sudan savanna, sahel savanna
guinea savanna, mangrove swamp, sahel savanna, sudan savanna
questions.explanation: Nigeria's vegetation transitions from coastal mangrove swamp, through tropical rainforest, into the progressively drier guinea, sudan, and sahel savanna belts moving from south to north.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: The River Niger enters Nigeria from the north-west, having originated in which country?
questions.explanation: The River Niger originates in the Fouta Djallon highlands of Guinea, flowing through Mali, Niger, and Benin before entering Nigeria.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: The River Benue, one of Nigeria's major rivers and a key tributary of the River Niger, originates mainly in the highlands of
questions.explanation: The River Benue rises in the Adamawa highlands of Cameroon before flowing westward into Nigeria and joining the River Niger at Lokoja.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: The Sokoto Plains, located in north-western Nigeria, are drained primarily by the
questions.explanation: The Sokoto Plains in north-western Nigeria are drained principally by the Sokoto and Rima rivers, which eventually join the River Niger.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.text: The Mambilla Plateau, one of Nigeria's highest and coolest highland regions, is located in which present-day state?
questions.explanation: The Mambilla Plateau, notable for its cool climate and highland tea plantations, is located in Taraba State in eastern Nigeria, near the border with Cameroon.
